core.title: Define the decision loop
core.text: The agent is the decision-maker; the environment applies the consequences of its actions. A state summarizes the information available when choosing, an action is a controllable choice, and a reward is feedback about the resulting transition. A trading environment can include market observations, execution, costs, and portfolio accounting; it need not consist only of the external market.

core.title: Why decisions are sequential
core.text: An action can change holdings, battery, queues, or time remaining, which changes the consequences and feasibility of later actions. A locally attractive gross return or shortest route need not maximize cumulative net reward. The relevant state therefore often includes information generated by the agent’s own past choices.

core.title: Prediction and control answer different questions
core.text: Supervised learning fits supplied targets such as return or sentiment labels. RL estimates the consequences of actions from reward-bearing transitions and uses them to choose behavior. A supervised forecast may supply an RL state feature, and logged transitions can support policy learning; neither calling a label BUY nor putting rows in time order makes a supervised task RL.

core.title: Episodes, credit, and policy
core.text: An episode has modeled start and stopping rules; reaching a goal, forced liquidation, or a time cap can end a run. A continuing task can still be analyzed in daily chunks. Delayed rewards create credit-assignment problems because several earlier choices may contribute. A policy is the action-selection rule, deterministic or stochastic; a Q-table supplies estimates on which different policies may act.

core.title: Choose the formulation for the objective
core.text: RL is useful when actions have meaningful cumulative consequences and relevant experience can be obtained. Simulator fidelity, interaction cost, coverage, and safe deployment determine whether that formulation is practical. A fixed-label sentiment task is usually supervised classification; sequential rebalancing with turnover is a natural control problem. In reversed items, judge the claim first, then invert the marked True/False selection.

groups.title: Agent, Environment, State, Action, and Reward
rules: Classify each quantity by its role: observation/state, chosen action, or resulting reward.
Include portfolio accounting and execution rules in the environment when they determine outcomes.
Use a reward that reflects the stated goal, such as net value change or negative implementation shortfall.
traps: A useful market observation is not automatically a reward.
The person who defines the task is not necessarily the agent acting in it.

groups.title: Sequential Decision-Making
rules: Evaluate choices through the states and opportunities they create later.
Include current inventory or resource capacity when it affects future costs and feasible actions.
Immediate gross gain can conflict with cumulative net gain or successful completion.
traps: Independent daily optimization can overlook turnover and inventory accumulation.
A fixed number of decisions does not make their order irrelevant.

groups.title: Reinforcement Learning vs. Supervised Learning
rules: A supervised learner consumes supplied targets; RL consumes reward-bearing state-action transitions.
Shared input indicators do not make objectives, targets, or outputs equivalent.
Combine supervised perception or forecasts with a policy when each serves a distinct purpose.
traps: Renaming labels BUY and SELL does not create reinforcement learning.
High classification accuracy does not guarantee the highest net policy return.

groups.title: Episodes and Continuing Tasks
rules: Define initialization, termination, truncation, and any forced liquidation explicitly.
A reporting boundary does not by itself reset a continuing task.
Changing reset frequency can change trading costs and delayed consequences.
traps: The end of one episode is not the end of all training.
Treating an artificial time cap as a genuine terminal event can change value targets; specify which task is modeled.

groups.title: Delayed Rewards and Credit Assignment
rules: Connect a delayed outcome to all earlier actions that contributed to it.
Zero rewards before a rare terminal payoff provide sparse informative feedback.
Evaluate shaping rewards for loops, shortcuts, and changes to the intended objective.
traps: The most recent action need not deserve all credit or blame.
Paying for activity alone can reward motion or turnover instead of progress.

groups.title: Policies and Action Selection
rules: A policy maps states to actions or action probabilities.
Value estimates and the decision rule that uses them are distinct.
Deterministic tie-breaking and fixed values are needed for reproducible greedy actions.
traps: A handwritten rule is still a policy.
A deterministic environment can be controlled by a stochastic policy.

groups.title: When Reinforcement Learning Is Appropriate
rules: Use sequential control when present choices alter future rewards, constraints, or decision context.
Use supervised learning when the immediate task is reproducing supplied targets.
Weigh the expected benefit of RL against the cost of collecting, validating, and deploying experience.
traps: A time series is not automatically an RL task.
Recognizing a sequential problem does not make unrestricted live exploration appropriate.

formulas.name: RL interaction
formulas.conditions: The action is selected from current information; reward and successor state arrive after the transition.

formulas.name: Cumulative objective
formulas.conditions: Specify the horizon, reward definition, and reset rules before comparing policies.

formulas.name: Greedy policy
formulas.conditions: Argmax returns an action; max returns its value. Ties require a stated rule.

examples.title: Map an execution task
examples.prompt: A parent order has 800 shares and 4 minutes left; the spread is 2 cents. The algorithm submits 200 shares and later observes $6 of implementation shortfall.
examples.work: Remaining quantity, time, and spread are state inputs. Submitting 200 shares is the action. Execution and accounting are environment dynamics; a reward of −$6 penalizes the shortfall.
examples.result: The mapping determines what information and objective the controller uses.

examples.title: Delayed feedback can reverse a local ranking
examples.prompt: Suppose a held position earns rewards −2, +4, +4 over three steps; staying in cash earns zero. Use γ = 0.9.
examples.work: The held position’s return is −2 + 0.9×4 + 0.9²×4 = 4.84. Its first reward is negative, but the complete discounted sequence is positive.
examples.result: An early cost does not by itself make a sequential decision poor.

domains.subject: ML
domains.title: Markov Decision Processes, Policies, and Values

core.title: A state must summarize relevant history
core.text: The Markov property says that the conditional distribution of the next state and reward depends on the current state and action, without needing extra past information. It is a sufficiency requirement, not a requirement to store every observation. Omitting package status, pending obligations, or holdings can merge contexts whose actions have different consequences.

core.title: Transitions describe uncertainty
core.text: For a fixed state-action pair, transition probabilities distribute mass across possible successor states and sum to one. Deterministic dynamics put all mass on one outcome. A deterministic policy cannot remove stochastic environment outcomes; an observed result also does not establish causation or change a probability to one.

core.title: Reward, return, and discounting
core.text: Reward is one transition’s feedback; return aggregates future rewards with an explicit time convention. The first reward has weight one, then γ, γ², and so on. A larger γ makes distant outcomes relatively more influential, including delayed losses. Finite tasks with finite rewards can use γ = 1; continuing undiscounted sums require additional care.

core.title: Values depend on future behavior
core.text: Vπ(s) is expected return from a state under policy π. Qπ(s,a) is expected return after choosing a particular action and then following π. Vπ averages the policy’s action values, whereas a greedy rule chooses a maximizing action. Expectations summarize distributions; they are neither guaranteed outcomes nor transition probabilities.

core.title: Bellman reasoning is a consistency relation
core.text: Compare immediate reward plus discounted expected continuation value, including every possible successor weighted by its probability. Greedy improvement is supported when the values and assumptions are sound. Choosing the largest incomplete or biased estimate is not a certificate of global optimality.

groups.title: States and the Markov Property
rules: A Markov state summarizes the information needed for relevant next-state and reward distributions.
Include omitted context when it changes action consequences or constraints.
A compact sufficient summary can replace raw history.
traps: The most important variable need not be a sufficient state.
Past information is not irrelevant merely because it occurred earlier.

groups.title: State Transitions and Environment Dynamics
rules: Condition transition probabilities on both state and action.
Sum probabilities over all possible successors to one.
Separate random market outcomes from deterministic changes to the agent’s holdings.
traps: Stochasticity does not imply the agent has no influence.
One realized successor does not prove a deterministic causal effect.

groups.title: Rewards, Returns, and Objectives
rules: Distinguish an immediate reward from the return over a sequence.
Use the specified numerical reward to determine the optimized objective.
Include costs and relevant risk consequences when the stated objective requires them.
traps: Penalties are rewards with negative sign.
Convergence cannot repair an incorrectly specified objective.

groups.title: Discount Factor and Time Preference
rules: Weight the first reward by one and each later reward by an additional factor of γ.
Low γ emphasizes near-term outcomes; high γ emphasizes delayed gains and losses.
Finite-horizon undiscounted sums can be valid.
traps: γ does not rescale the first reward.
A larger γ is not a promise of higher realized profit.

groups.title: State-Value Functions
rules: Compute state value as expected return under the specified policy.
Weight every outcome, including less likely losses.
Allow different policies to assign different values to the same state.
traps: The most likely payoff is not generally the expected value.
Zero current reward need not mean zero future value.

groups.title: Action-Value Functions
rules: A Q-value fixes the first action and includes specified continuation behavior.
For a stochastic policy, average Q-values using action probabilities.
For greedy selection, compare all candidate Q-values within the same state.
traps: Q-values do not need to sum to one.
A negative expectation does not imply every realized trade loses.

groups.title: Bellman Reasoning and Optimal Policies
rules: Add immediate reward to discounted expected successor value.
A local policy-improvement step chooses a better-valued action under the available estimates.
Optimality claims require appropriate dynamics, rewards, coverage, and value accuracy.
traps: Do not compare successor values while ignoring different immediate rewards.
One improved state does not prove the entire policy is optimal.

formulas.name: Markov sufficiency
formulas.formula: P(s_(t+1), r_(t+1) | history, a_t) = P(s_(t+1), r_(t+1) | s_t, a_t)
formulas.conditions: Equality is a modeling assumption about the chosen state representation.

formulas.name: Discounted return
formulas.conditions: For finite H and finite rewards, γ = 1 is permitted. For bounded continuing rewards, γ < 1 gives an absolutely convergent sum.

formulas.name: State and action values
formulas.formula: Vπ(s) = Σ_a π(a|s)Qπ(s,a); Qπ(s,a) = E[r + γVπ(s′) | s,a]
formulas.conditions: The same continuation policy π must be used in both quantities.

formulas.name: Bellman optimality
formulas.conditions: The expectation accounts for stochastic transitions; a true terminal state has no future reward.

examples.title: Expected value is not the most likely payoff
examples.prompt: State A yields return 10 with probability 0.8 and −10 with probability 0.2; State B yields 5 for certain.
examples.work: V(A) = 0.8×10 + 0.2×(−10) = 6; V(B) = 5. An expected-return objective ranks A higher despite its downside outcome.
examples.result: A is worth 6 in expectation, not a guaranteed 10.

examples.title: One-step Bellman comparison
examples.prompt: Safe gives 2 now then value 5. Risky gives 0 now then value 10 or −2 with equal probability. Let γ = 0.9.
examples.work: Safe: 2 + 0.9×5 = 6.5. Risky successor expectation: 0.5×10 + 0.5×(−2) = 4; total: 0 + 0.9×4 = 3.6.
examples.result: Choose Safe under these estimates.

examples.title: Average over the policy
examples.prompt: A policy selects A with probability 0.75 and B with probability 0.25; Qπ(s,A)=8 and Qπ(s,B)=0.
examples.work: Vπ(s) = 0.75×8 + 0.25×0 = 6. Using max would answer a different action-selection question.
examples.result: The current policy’s state value is 6.

core.title: Read a Q-table correctly
core.text: Each row identifies a represented state and each column an available action. Entries estimate cumulative action values, not immediate rewards, probabilities, or exact successors. Greedy selection compares a row; ties are resolved by an implementation rule. An unvisited row still reflects initialization, even if its entries look numerically plausible.

core.title: The update blends old knowledge with a target
core.text: For observed (s,a,r,s′), standard Q-learning forms y = r + γ max_a′ Q(s′,a′). It then changes only Q(s,a) by α[y − Q(s,a)]. The TD error may be negative even when the successor value is positive. The target is one sample using current estimates; repeated representative transitions are needed in stochastic settings.

core.title: α, γ, and exploration have different jobs
core.text: The learning rate α controls how strongly a new target changes the old estimate: zero freezes it, one replaces it. The discount factor γ controls the weight of future rewards inside the target. Epsilon governs behavioral exploration. A high constant α reacts quickly but remains noisy; a declining schedule supports stationary estimation, while a positive rate can allow adaptation to change.

core.title: Off-policy bootstrapping
core.text: Q-learning bootstraps from the maximum next-state estimate even when the behavior policy next chooses a different exploratory action. That separates the behavior policy collecting data from the greedy target policy. A true terminal transition uses target r alone; it must not bootstrap from the reset state of the next episode. Max over noisy estimates can propagate overestimation.

core.title: Convergence needs more than stability
core.text: For tabular stationary finite problems, sufficient repeated visitation and suitable learning-rate conditions support convergence results. A flat curve, unchanged actions, optimistic initialization, or one visit per pair is not a proof. Sparse coverage, hidden state, nonstationarity, and biased simulations weaken any conclusion drawn from small numerical updates.

groups.title: Q-Table Structure and Interpretation
rules: Use one value per state-action pair and compare actions within the current row.
Q estimates expected cumulative return under the represented continuation behavior.
State the tie-breaking rule when extracting a greedy policy.
traps: Negative Q can still be the largest value in a row.
A high value in one row does not rank that action in every state.

groups.title: Temporal-Difference Update
rules: Compute the target, then the TD error, then the weighted update.
Update the previous state-action pair using the observed reward and successor.
Repeated transitions can revise the same entry without an explicit transition model.
traps: A negative reward need not replace the entire estimate.
One actual sample is not an exact expected value.

groups.title: Learning Rate
rules: α weights new targets against the existing estimate.
α = 0 freezes; α = 1 adopts the sample target.
Large constant α emphasizes recent outcomes and can retain noise; smaller α adapts more slowly.
traps: Constant α is not an equal-weight mean of all historical samples.
No fixed learning rate guarantees the best final policy across tasks.

groups.title: Discount Factor in Q-Learning
rules: γ weights the successor term while leaving immediate reward undiscounted.
γ = 0 still leaves an α-weighted immediate-reward update.
Changing γ can alter the preferred policy without changing the reward function.
traps: γ is not the random-action rate.
γ = 1 does not imply divergence in every finite episodic task.

groups.title: Maximum Future Q-Value
rules: Use the maximum available successor estimate in standard Q-learning.
For a true terminal transition, set future contribution to zero.
Noisy inflated maxima can contaminate predecessor estimates through bootstrapping.
traps: The selected exploratory next action need not supply the Q-learning target.
The maximum estimate is not proof of the maximum true value.

groups.title: Off-Policy Learning
rules: Separate the behavior that samples experience from the policy represented in the target.
Exploratory actions can provide useful evidence about good and bad alternatives.
A max-successor target differs from bootstrapping on the actually selected next action.
traps: Off-policy does not mean learning without adequate state-action coverage.
Using a Q-table does not by itself make an algorithm on-policy.

groups.title: Initialization, Visitation, and Convergence
rules: Inspect visitation counts alongside Q-values and learned actions.
Initialization can strongly influence early greedy behavior.
Require sustained representative coverage and suitable update conditions before making convergence claims.
traps: An unchanged unvisited row contains initialization, not learned evidence.
Optimistic initialization does not guarantee exploration of every reachable pair.

formulas.name: TD target and error
formulas.formula: y = r + γ max_a′ Q(s′,a′); δ = y − Q(s,a)
formulas.conditions: Use y = r for a genuinely terminal transition. A time-limit truncation needs the task’s explicit continuation convention.

formulas.name: Q-learning update
formulas.conditions: Other table entries remain unchanged in a single direct tabular update; 0 ≤ α ≤ 1 is the usual blending range.

formulas.name: Learning-rate convergence conditions
formulas.conditions: These conditions apply per repeatedly visited pair for a finite stationary Markov task with bounded rewards and γ < 1; suitable episodic variants need their own termination assumptions. Merely decreasing α is not enough.

formulas.name: Greedy action
formulas.conditions: Break ties explicitly. The value max Q is a number; argmax identifies an action.

examples.title: Positive TD update
examples.prompt: Old Q = 2, reward = 1, γ = 0.9, max successor Q = 4, α = 0.5.
examples.result: New Q is 3.3, halfway between 2 and 4.6.

examples.title: Negative TD update
examples.prompt: Old Q = 5, reward = −2, max successor Q = 3, γ = 0.5, α = 0.2.
examples.result: A positive successor estimate does not prevent the current value from falling.

examples.title: Terminal reward counted once
examples.prompt: A goal transition pays 20 and terminates; old Q = 8, α = 0.25, γ = 0.9.
examples.work: No reward remains after termination, so y = 20 and Q_new = 8 + 0.25×(20 − 8) = 11.
examples.result: New Q is 11; do not add the reward again or bootstrap from the next episode.

core.title: Exploration buys information
core.text: Exploitation selects the currently highest estimated action. Exploration tries alternatives that may be worse now but can improve later decisions. Early lucky samples can make an inferior action look best, while continual heavy randomness can reduce realized performance even after values are useful. The right balance depends on how much future use the information will receive.

core.title: Read the exact epsilon convention
core.text: In the common implementation, the exploratory branch samples uniformly from all actions, so it can select the greedy action too. Other implementations sample only nongreedy actions. Ties in the greedy set add another source of randomness. Epsilon is a branch probability, not the marginal probability assigned to every action.

core.title: Decay does not certify coverage
core.text: A geometric schedule reduces random actions, but fast decay can freeze early mistakes. A positive floor preserves opportunities to sample alternatives, yet it cannot make unreachable states reachable or ensure equal visitation. State coverage and state-action coverage differ, and one sample per pair can miss stochastic variability or rare losses.

core.title: Measure learning and deployment separately
core.text: A flat training reward curve can reflect adequate learning, poor exploration, or a restrictive state representation. Compare seeds and held-out policies, with controlled tie-breaking and fixed preprocessing. Greedy evaluation can remove deliberate exploration; it does not make inaccurate values correct or eliminate environment randomness.

core.title: Distinguish noise from change
core.text: A stationary stochastic environment can produce different outcomes from the same pair while its distribution stays fixed. Nonstationarity changes the distribution itself, for example when trading costs rise. Frozen Q-values do not adapt; retraining or online updating can respond but introduces estimation noise and, with exploration, real costs.

groups.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
rules: Exploitation follows the best current estimate; exploration acquires evidence about alternatives.
Judge exploratory choices by possible information benefits as well as immediate reward.
Too much exploration can depress deployment reward despite accurate values.
traps: The current leader may be an estimation error.
One disappointing trial does not fully characterize a stochastic alternative.

groups.title: Epsilon-Greedy Action Selection
rules: Inspect whether the exploratory set includes the greedy action.
Add probability from every branch that can produce a given action.
Account separately for ties among maximizing actions.
traps: ε is not the probability of each nongreedy action.
ε = 0 removes exploration but not random greedy tie-breaking.

groups.title: Exploration Decay
rules: For multiplicative decay, apply the decay factor once per stated step.
Fast decay can leave useful alternatives untested.
A positive floor preserves residual exploration, with a continuing short-term cost.
traps: Positive geometric decay does not reach exactly zero in finite exact-arithmetic steps.
A floor does not guarantee equal or sufficient visitation.

groups.title: State-Action Coverage
rules: Count state-action pairs, not just distinct states.
Exploratory choices may unlock downstream states a greedy route never reaches.
Use repeated samples when rewards and transitions are stochastic.
traps: Unvisited does not necessarily mean unreachable.
One visit per pair is nominal coverage, not accurate estimation.

groups.title: Premature Convergence and Local Behavior
rules: Consider early-sample luck when behavior stabilizes rapidly.
Use multiple seeds and validation evidence to assess sensitivity.
Check alternative actions and coverage before treating a flat curve as completion.
traps: The majority policy across seeds need not be the best.
Longer training alone is not a global-optimality guarantee.

groups.title: Training vs. Deployment Behavior
rules: Separate training exploration from the behavior being evaluated or deployed.
Freeze values, preprocessing, and tie rules for a fixed-policy evaluation.
Report variability if the evaluated policy intentionally remains stochastic.
traps: The deployment epsilon need not equal the training epsilon.
Greedy actions can still be poor when values are inaccurate.

groups.title: Nonstationary and Stochastic Environments
rules: Different realized outcomes can occur under a fixed stochastic distribution.
Changing transition or reward distributions can make historical values stale.
Monitor drift and assess the costs of adaptation and residual exploration.
traps: Random reward variation alone does not prove regime change.
Nonzero epsilon does not instantly detect every environmental change.

formulas.name: Uniform exploration over all actions
formulas.formula: P(unique greedy action) = 1−ε+ε/m; P(each nongreedy action) = ε/m
formulas.conditions: There are m actions and a unique greedy action. If k actions tie and greedy ties are uniform, each tied action gets (1−ε)/k + ε/m.

formulas.name: Exploration excludes the greedy action
formulas.conditions: Applies only to the stated nongreedy-only exploratory branch with one greedy action.

formulas.name: Geometric decay
formulas.formula: ε_n = ε_0 d^n; with floor: ε_n = max(ε_min, ε_0 d^n)
formulas.conditions: Count decay events, not raw decisions unless the implementation decays after every decision; 0 < d < 1.

formulas.name: Tabular coverage
formulas.formula: Total entries = |S|×|A|; pair coverage = visited pairs / total entries
formulas.conditions: Counts alone do not measure sample quality, rare-outcome coverage, or deployment reachability.

examples.title: Exploration can choose the greedy action
examples.prompt: Three actions, ε = 0.20, a unique greedy action, and uniform exploratory sampling over all three.
examples.work: Greedy probability = 0.80 + 0.20/3 = 0.8667. Each other action receives 0.20/3 = 0.0667. The probabilities sum to one.
examples.result: 86.67% greedy selection, despite an 80% greedy branch.

examples.title: A different implementation gives different probabilities
examples.prompt: Four actions, ε = 0.40, and exploration samples only the three nongreedy actions.
examples.work: Greedy selection has probability 0.60. Each other action has probability 0.40/3 ≈ 0.1333.
examples.result: Always read the sampling set before calculating probabilities.

examples.title: Decay versus evidence
examples.prompt: Begin at ε = 0.80 and multiply by 0.90 after each episode. What is epsilon after three decays?
examples.work: ε_3 = 0.80×0.90³ = 0.5832. The number describes the exploratory branch probability, not how many pairs have been adequately sampled.
examples.result: 58.32% after three decay events.

core.title: Dyna combines acting, modeling, and planning
core.text: Plain Q-learning can update from a real transition without learning an environment model. Dyna-Q adds a model of next states and rewards, then samples model-generated transitions for extra Q-updates. These simulated transitions reuse existing information; they are not new external observations or fresh realized profits.

core.title: Represent the dynamics you actually observe
core.text: A deterministic stationary transition can be stored as one successor and reward for each observed pair. Stochastic environments require a distribution or another representation of variability. Normalized successor counts estimate transition probabilities, and a reward model can estimate an average rather than the last noisy observation. Unknown pairs need explicit treatment instead of invented default transitions.

core.title: Planning spreads information through the table
core.text: After a real update and model update, each planning step selects a modeled pair, generates a successor and reward, and applies the usual TD rule. A newly discovered terminal reward can spread to predecessor values without physically traversing the entire route again. Which pairs are sampled and in what order affects propagation speed.

core.title: Sample efficiency is not free computation
core.text: Dyna can improve the policy using fewer costly real interactions, at the price of more computation per interaction. More planning is attractive when an accurate model is cheap relative to acting. If direct simulation is already inexpensive or model construction is inaccurate and costly, the practical benefit can disappear.

core.title: Planning repeats model assumptions, including mistakes
core.text: Extensive planning can amplify omitted costs, stale routes, optimistic tails, and missing rare outcomes. More replays of a biased model do not create corrective evidence. Continued direct observation, targeted coverage, and model validation remain necessary, especially after environmental change.

groups.title: Direct vs. Simulated Experience
rules: Direct experience comes from the external environment; planning generates transitions internally.
Both types can drive the same Q-learning update.
Planning can revisit an older modeled pair instead of only the most recent real pair.
traps: Fifty planning steps are not fifty independent market observations.
Model-free direct Q-learning does not require a learned transition table.

groups.title: Transition Model Learning
rules: Store deterministic successors only when that representation matches the dynamics.
Use outcome counts or probabilities when one pair has multiple possible successors.
Restrict empirical replay to supported pairs or make any assumptions about unobserved pairs explicit.
traps: The latest observed outcome is not the full stochastic distribution.
Replaying an old route does not prove it is still open.

groups.title: Reward Model Learning
rules: A reward model supplies the immediate reward estimate for a simulated target.
Average representative noisy rewards when expected reward is the desired model.
Revise the model if costs or reward behavior change.
traps: An accurate transition model does not imply an accurate reward model.
A modeled reward is not a fresh external payoff.

groups.title: Dyna Planning Updates
rules: Perform a direct Q-update, update the model, then run the configured planning updates.
Use the same α and γ logic in simulated TD updates.
Relevant predecessor replay can propagate a discovered reward backward.
traps: dyna = 0 leaves ordinary direct Q-learning in place.
One replay does not instantly solve every upstream state.

groups.title: Sample Efficiency
rules: Measure real interactions needed to reach a learning target separately from compute cost.
Planning can reuse scarce or expensive direct observations.
Compare model cost and fidelity against the cost of obtaining more direct experience.
traps: More internal updates do not create independent information.
Model-based learning does not guarantee superiority on every run.

groups.title: Model Error and Planning Bias
rules: Planning propagates the transition and reward errors already present in the model.
Fresh direct observations are needed to discover unmodeled changes.
Reducing planning can limit amplification but does not correct the underlying bias.
traps: Thousands of optimistic replays do not prove positive true expected return.
Nonstationarity can invalidate both the policy and its internal model.

groups.title: Dyna in Deterministic and Stochastic Environments
rules: A deterministic table can exactly represent observed stationary deterministic pairs.
For stochastic outcomes, estimate and sample the categorical successor distribution.
Continue collecting evidence about rare outcomes and previously unvisited pairs.
traps: No observed rare penalty does not imply zero probability.
A sampled next state is an outcome, not necessarily the expected next-state representation.

formulas.name: Transition model from counts
formulas.conditions: The denominator must be positive. Lecture pseudocounts avoid division by zero but encode a prior, not evidence of observed outcomes.

formulas.name: Reward-model update
formulas.conditions: The lecture uses a learning-rate blend. Constant β emphasizes recent rewards; β = 1/n gives a running mean over n observations for a fixed pair.

formulas.name: Dyna computation per real transition
formulas.formula: Q-updates per real step = 1 + d; total = N_real(1+d)
formulas.conditions: Assumes exactly one direct update and d planning updates per real transition. Model updates are additional bookkeeping.

formulas.name: Planning target
formulas.conditions: Generate the modeled successor and reward from the selected pair. True terminal modeled transitions omit the future term.

examples.title: Count updates without inventing data
examples.prompt: An agent gets 200 real transitions and performs dyna = 20 planning steps after each.
examples.work: Direct Q-updates = 200. Planning updates = 200×20 = 4,000. Total Q-updates = 4,200, all based on only 200 real transitions.
examples.result: More updates can improve sample efficiency but do not create 4,200 independent observations.

examples.title: Estimate a stochastic model
examples.prompt: From one pair, a model records 50 up, 20 flat, and 30 down outcomes.
examples.work: Total count = 100; estimated probabilities are 0.50, 0.20, and 0.30. Planning may sample any of the three outcomes using those probabilities.
examples.result: A single last-outcome record would discard the estimated distribution.

examples.title: A rare event can be missing by chance
examples.prompt: An action has an independent 1% severe-penalty probability per trial. No penalty appears in the first 50 trials.
examples.work: P(no penalty in 50 trials) = 0.99^50 ≈ 0.605. Missing the event is therefore quite plausible. Replaying only the observed safe outcome cannot reveal it.
examples.result: Absence in 50 samples is weak evidence of safety, not proof that the true probability is zero.

domains.subject: ML
domains.title: State Representation, Discretization, and Reward Design

core.title: Choose sufficient, available information
core.text: State features should help distinguish consequences, constraints, or valuable actions and must be available at decision time. Momentum, volatility, event status, inventory, and remaining time can each matter. Adding random identifiers or many redundant indicators increases complexity without necessarily improving decisions; adding tomorrow’s outcome creates leakage.

core.title: Discretization trades detail for evidence per state
core.text: Binning maps continuous observations into a finite set of labels. Fixed thresholds retain fixed numeric meaning but can become imbalanced after a distribution shift. Rank-based thresholds spread reference observations across bins but change meaning with the reference distribution. Fit thresholds using permitted historical data, define boundary behavior, and apply the intended deployment convention consistently.

core.title: The Cartesian product grows quickly
core.text: With b bins for each of k indicators, the nominal market-state space is b^k. Holdings and other dimensions multiply it further, and each action needs a separate value. Fine bins can separate meaningful contexts but produce sparse visitation; coarse bins pool experience but can merge contexts needing different actions. Not every nominal combination must be reachable.

core.title: Aliasing is missing decision information
core.text: Two observations share a state label when the learner cannot distinguish them. That is harmful when their dynamics, rewards, or feasible actions differ. Inventory direction alone may be insufficient if position magnitude changes risk limits. Adding relevant context or a useful history summary can help approximate Markov sufficiency, but neither a larger table nor a higher learning rate recovers information absent from the state.

core.title: Rewards specify incentives, not aspirations
core.text: Realized-only P&L delays feedback while open positions can gain or lose economic value. Mark-to-market net value changes provide denser feedback but still need appropriate risk objectives and timing. Penalties and bonuses can change the optimal policy: extreme turnover penalties may cause inactivity, and flat-position bonuses may encourage costly liquidation-and-reentry cycles. Audit full behavior rather than one rewarded metric.

groups.title: State Feature Selection
rules: Keep features available at decision time and relevant to future actions, outcomes, or constraints.
Treat current holdings and time remaining as legitimate state features.
Balance added information against redundancy, sparse visitation, and limited data.
traps: Training-file availability does not imply live availability.
A univariate historical correlation does not guarantee policy value.

groups.title: Continuous-to-Discrete State Mapping
rules: Define numeric thresholds and inclusion at each boundary.
Expect multiple raw observations to map to the same finite label.
Fit threshold statistics on allowed reference data and consider boundary noise.
traps: Bins do not preserve exact distances or all economic distinctions.
Balanced reference counts do not guarantee equal deployment counts or an optimal state.

groups.title: Granularity and State-Space Size
rules: Multiply bin counts across dimensions to get nominal combinations.
Multiply by action count to size a Q-table.
Refine decision-relevant dimensions selectively when broad refinement would exhaust coverage.
traps: Doubling every dimension’s bins multiplies states exponentially in dimension count.
Larger tables do not supply their own training observations.

groups.title: State Aliasing and Missing Information
rules: Look for identical encoded states with materially different action consequences.
Add available context or history summaries that distinguish those cases.
Recognize that any summary can still omit relevant hidden information.
traps: Perfect measurement of included variables does not make an incomplete state sufficient.
Raising α cannot reveal a missing direction, event flag, or hidden condition.

groups.title: Position and Holdings as State
rules: Include current position when order size, cost, or feasibility depends on holdings.
Represent position magnitude or capacity if sign alone merges different constraint states.
Check executed holdings and enforce hard limits independently of the learned policy.
traps: Agent-controlled information can belong in state.
Adding holdings does not guarantee that the learner stops overtrading.

groups.title: Reward Definition
rules: Distinguish realized P&L from total economic value change.
Incorporate commissions and impact when optimizing net results.
Align reward scale, timing, discounting, and risk treatment with the long-run objective.
traps: Zero realized profit does not mean zero economic change.
Cumulative learning cannot turn an arbitrary reward into risk-adjusted growth automatically.

groups.title: Reward Shaping and Unintended Incentives
rules: Evaluate shaping terms for changes in incentives and complete portfolio outcomes.
Calibrate penalties to actual costs or an explicitly intended preference.
Check for activity loops, excessive inactivity, and liquidation/reentry behavior.
traps: Reward maximization can succeed while the human objective fails.
Arbitrary shaping is not guaranteed to preserve the optimal policy.

formulas.name: Nominal state-space size
formulas.conditions: b_j is the bin count of feature j, h is the number of holdings states; nominal combinations can include unreachable states.

formulas.name: Mixed-radix state index
formulas.conditions: Three-feature example: i_j is the zero-based bin index and B_j its bin count. Extend by nesting for more dimensions. Equal ten-bin dimensions can be encoded like decimal digits.

formulas.name: Daily economic reward
formulas.conditions: Specify the valuation and execution times; include realized and unrealized P&L, deduct costs once, and adjust for external cash flows if present.

formulas.name: Illustrative shaped reward
formulas.conditions: This is a design choice and can change the optimal policy; λ and bonuses require economic validation.

examples.title: Doubling bins multiplies complexity
examples.prompt: Four indicators move from 5 bins each to 10 bins each; the same history is used.
examples.work: Old market states = 5^4 = 625. New states = 10^4 = 10,000. Ratio = 16. With 3 holdings states and 3 actions, entries rise from 5,625 to 90,000.
examples.result: Sixteen times as many entries require much more evidence for comparable coverage.

examples.title: The same signal can imply different orders
examples.prompt: For target +1,000 shares, compare portfolios currently at 0, +1,000, and −1,000 shares.
examples.work: Required orders are +1,000, 0, and +2,000 shares. The market signal can be identical while costs and feasibility differ.
examples.result: Holdings distinguish entering, maintaining, and reversing a position.

examples.title: A reward loop that misses the task
examples.prompt: A robot earns +1 for each forward move toward the goal and 0 for moving backward; it alternates forward and backward without finishing.
examples.work: Each two-action cycle earns +1 despite zero net progress. Ten cycles earn +10 while completion never occurs. A symmetric net-progress measure would make the cycle’s net progress zero.
examples.result: The agent exploits the numerical reward; completion and full-path behavior must be checked.

core.title: Market state must respect the clock
core.text: A daily trading state can combine discretized indicators with current holdings and constraints. Use only information available when the action is selected, including the permitted publication time of external data. Full-history normalization, future returns in indicators, and test-based bin selection contaminate a claimed out-of-sample evaluation.

core.title: An action is not necessarily an order
core.text: If actions specify target positions, order quantity equals desired holdings minus current holdings. Choosing long while already long can require no trade; switching short to long crosses zero and trades twice the position magnitude. Order clipping or rejection can leave actual holdings different from requested targets, so the environment must report the realized state.

core.title: Positions persist and generate rewards
core.text: Holding an asset can change portfolio value even on days with no orders. A reward based only on position closure delays economic feedback; daily net value changes include unrealized P&L. The action comes first, then its interval’s outcome is observed. Future outcomes may be realized rewards later, but cannot be supplied as earlier decision features.

core.title: Costs change the decision problem
core.text: Commissions and impact affect the value of trading and therefore can change Q-value rankings. Frequent reversals can erase a small gross advantage. Training on gross rewards and evaluating only net results can produce a systematically misaligned policy; cost-aware training can rationally suppress marginal trades without implying that the learner failed.

core.title: Evaluate the policy that will actually run
core.text: Fit features, thresholds, rewards, and hyperparameters on training and development periods. For a frozen-policy test, keep values and preprocessing fixed and use an untouched later period. Repeated tuning on a test makes it development data. Monitor later state frequencies, costs, and outcomes: stable actions do not imply stable profitability, and neither rolling retraining nor online adaptation guarantees improvement.

groups.title: Mapping Market Data into States
rules: Build state from available indicators, portfolio information, and constraints.
Fit preprocessing and choose bins without using held-out outcomes.
Check coverage and aliasing after discretization.
traps: A historical-price formula can still leak if its window includes future observations.
Sharing a bin does not establish identical future-return distributions.

groups.title: Mapping Actions into Trades or Positions
rules: Specify whether an action is an incremental order or a desired target.
Translate targets using current executed holdings.
Apply feasibility constraints and pass actual execution outcomes back into state.
traps: HOLD need not mean cash.
A target action does not remove commission, impact, or liquidity constraints.

groups.title: Holdings, Inventory, and Position Persistence
rules: Allow positions to persist across decisions without repeated orders.
Include holdings detail sufficient for costs, risk, and capacity.
Account for P&L on held positions even when trade quantity is zero.
traps: No order is not the same as no exposure or zero reward.
Long/cash/short labels can alias very different position sizes.

groups.title: Trading Rewards and Portfolio Value
rules: Reward timing must follow the economic interval being measured.
Use net total portfolio value when the objective includes open-position gains, losses, and costs.
Distinguish dollar reward from percentage return using starting value.
traps: A realized-only zero reward can hide an unrealized loss.
Paying for order count rewards activity even if the portfolio loses money.

groups.title: Transaction Costs, Impact, and Turnover
rules: Measure turnover from the actual position changes required by targets.
Train with relevant cost consequences when seeking net performance.
Recognize that removing marginal trades can be a rational response to costs.
traps: A reversal trades twice the one-sided position magnitude.
A positive gross opportunity need not remain positive after costs.

groups.title: Training, Testing, and Out-of-Sample Evaluation
rules: Use chronological training, selection, and untouched evaluation periods.
Freeze the policy and fitted preprocessing for a fixed-policy test.
Compare in-sample and out-of-sample performance with costs and benchmarks.
traps: Selecting among many runs on the test return overfits that test.
One poor test does not prove every RL trading design is useless.

groups.title: Market Nonstationarity and Policy Stability
rules: Compare recent state-action outcomes with historical estimates.
Monitor distribution, costs, turnover, performance, and realized holdings.
Validate retraining or online adaptation as its own deployment process.
traps: Unchanged actions do not prove unchanged market rewards.
Newer data and continuing exploration do not automatically improve performance.

formulas.name: Target-to-order mapping
formulas.conditions: Use executed holdings, not a previous requested target; clipping or partial fills can create a difference.

formulas.name: Net dollar reward and return
formulas.formula: r_t = V_end,net − V_start; R_t = r_t / V_start
formulas.conditions: Assumes no external cash flow and positive starting value. Do not subtract a commission twice if already included in net value.

formulas.name: Simple explicit cost model
formulas.conditions: Illustrative per-order commission c plus proportional impact η; actual question-specific execution conventions take precedence.

formulas.name: Three-indicator market states
formulas.conditions: Assumes all Cartesian combinations are encoded; count visitation separately.

examples.title: A reversal crosses through cash
examples.prompt: Current holdings are −1,000 shares and the action requests a +1,000-share target.
examples.work: ΔH = +1,000 − (−1,000) = +2,000 shares. By comparison, cash-to-long buys 1,000 and long-to-long buys zero.
examples.result: Buy 2,000 shares, with costs based on the actual reversal.

examples.title: Net reward in dollars and percent
examples.prompt: Start at $100,000. End value before a $50 commission is $101,000.
examples.result: The return is 0.95%, not 9.5%.

examples.title: Cost-aware opportunity threshold
examples.prompt: Suppose a reversal trades 2,000 shares at $50; commission is $10 and modeled impact is 0.1% of traded notional. Expected gross gain is $80.
examples.work: Notional = 2,000×$50 = $100,000. Impact = $100. Total cost = $110. Expected net gain = $80 − $110 = −$30.
examples.result: A gross-positive trade can be unattractive once execution costs enter the value.

core.title: Compare complete systems, not output labels
core.text: A tree strategy fits supplied labels or returns and then maps predictions into trades. A Q-learner estimates action values from reward-bearing transitions and extracts a policy. LONG is a decision, not necessarily a return forecast. The two can use the same indicators while differing in objectives, horizons, feedback, and portfolio-state access.

core.title: The forecast-to-trade step has its own economics
core.text: A return model and its decision threshold are distinct components. Changing a threshold can change positions without refitting the predictor, and a holdings-aware no-trade region can account for costs. Direct policy learning can encode these consequences in rewards, but neither architecture automatically aligns with net risk-adjusted performance.

core.title: Learning signals embed assumptions
core.text: Supervised labels specify a horizon, thresholds, and possibly costs or an oracle position rule. They legitimately use later outcomes within training, provided availability and split boundaries are respected. RL rewards depend on actions and holdings, and TD propagation assigns delayed credit. Matching feature names does not match these signals.

core.title: Historical replay is partly interactive
core.text: A fixed market history can still support sequential action-dependent holdings and rewards. Retained Q-values and changing exploration can produce different trajectories on repeated episodes. Those passes do not create independent market histories, and immutable recorded prices do not model the agent’s causal effect on future order flow.

core.title: Fair comparison requires aligned conditions
core.text: Align market information, timestamp availability, access to holdings, execution rules, capital, leverage, periods, costs, and metric conventions. Apply the same development discipline to manual rules and learned strategies. Report cumulative return, risk, drawdown, turnover, and benchmark-relative results on new data; one winning day, a small gross edge, or the strongest training score does not establish reliable economic superiority.

groups.title: Q-Learner vs. Decision-Tree Strategy Learner
rules: A tree fits supplied targets; a Q-learner updates values from rewards and transitions.
Document outputs, exploration, training passes, seeds, and stopping rules.
Treat identical market indicators as only one controlled aspect of the comparison.
traps: An RL action is not necessarily a numerical forecast.
Repeated RL episodes do not guarantee a globally optimal trading policy.

groups.title: Direct Policy Learning vs. Predict-Then-Trade
rules: Separate the predictor from the rule converting its output to a position.
Permit costs and holdings to influence the execution rule when they matter.
Evaluate net portfolio results instead of assuming forecast accuracy settles the comparison.
traps: A no-trade decision can be economically correct.
Predict-then-trade systems can incorporate costs too.

groups.title: Labels, Rewards, and Learning Signals
rules: Read label horizon, thresholds, and embedded cost assumptions.
Read reward timing, dependence on positions, and discounting.
Treat label construction and reward design as strategy choices.
traps: Future outcomes used only as training targets are not automatically leakage.
A negative initial reward does not establish a negative cumulative action value.

groups.title: Batch Learning vs. Interactive Learning
rules: Fixed prices can coexist with action-dependent portfolio transitions.
Retaining learned values across resets can change later training actions.
Describe which simulator variables respond to the agent.
traps: Repeated passes through one history are not independent market samples.
A fixed impact formula does not reproduce every live market feedback effect.

groups.title: Shared Features and Fair Inputs
rules: Align mathematical feature definitions, windows, and availability timestamps.
Compare complete information access, including holdings used by downstream decision rules.
Finalize manual thresholds using development data just as for learned parameters.
traps: Identical feature names do not imply identical information.
A manual rule can overfit a test chart.

groups.title: Fair Strategy Comparison
rules: Use aligned dates, starting capital, allowed leverage, execution, and costs.
Calculate the same metric set under the same conventions for each strategy.
Include a common benchmark and consider both risk and return.
traps: Dollar profit alone confounds capital and permitted exposure.
Common dates do not make incompatible ranking metrics comparable.

groups.title: Manual, Supervised, and RL Strategy Evaluation
rules: Evaluate the selected systems on unseen periods under matched conditions.
Distinguish win frequency, statistical reliability, and economic effect size.
Investigate sensitivity to regimes, randomness, turnover, and costs.
traps: One correct short trade cannot establish universal algorithm superiority.
Statistical significance would not by itself make a tiny net gain worthwhile.

formulas.name: Prediction-to-position rule
formulas.formula: H_target = +L if forecast > τ_buy; −L if forecast < τ_sell; otherwise use the specified cash/hold rule
formulas.conditions: Threshold and cash-versus-hold conventions are separate strategy parameters. Holdings-dependent bands can incorporate turnover costs.

formulas.name: Net economic difference
formulas.conditions: Use matched capital, horizons, exposure constraints, and consistent cost accounting before comparing.

formulas.name: Window win rate
formulas.conditions: A win rate alone omits magnitude, uncertainty, dependence across windows, and transaction costs.

examples.title: The threshold changes trades, not the forecast
examples.prompt: A fixed model forecasts a 0.15% next-day return. Its rule initially trades every positive prediction; a revised rule requires more than 0.20%.
examples.work: The forecast remains 0.15%. The zero-threshold rule trades; the 0.20% rule does not. If the modeled full trade cost is 0.20%, the simple expected net gain is −0.05% before other effects.
examples.result: A cost-aware decision layer can improve alignment without refitting the predictor.

examples.title: A small win count is not an economic edge
examples.prompt: A learner wins in 11 of 20 windows. Its average gross advantage is 0.03 percentage points per window, but extra costs average 0.05 points.
examples.work: Win rate = 11/20 = 55%. Average net difference = 0.03 − 0.05 = −0.02 percentage points per window. Win frequency does not supply a significance test or a positive net effect.
examples.result: The reported gross advantage disappears after costs.

core.title: A network is a parameterized computation
core.text: A dense unit combines inputs through weights and a bias, then applies an activation. Width counts units within a layer; depth counts successive layers. Equal total hidden-unit counts do not imply equal connectivity, parameter count, or represented function. An output’s interpretation depends on its target and loss, not merely whether it is a scalar.

core.title: Nonlinearity makes depth expressive
core.text: Composing affine maps without nonlinear activations remains one affine map, regardless of depth. Nonlinear activations allow richer learned representations. Sigmoid units with extreme pre-activations can saturate and yield small local derivatives, weakening earlier gradients. A visually interpretable hidden pattern does not by itself establish a causal financial mechanism.

core.title: Forward prediction is distinct from learning
core.text: A forward pass applies learned transformations to inputs and produces a score or forecast. Ordinary inference needs neither target labels nor a backward pass. Fixed parameters and deterministic evaluation operations produce the same output for the same input. Consistent preprocessing and correct evaluation mode matter; a downstream trade threshold can change while the network score stays fixed.

core.title: Loss and optimization specify what improves
core.text: The loss compares predictions with targets; MSE penalizes large errors quadratically, while classification losses address class probabilities and labels. Backpropagation computes gradients by the chain rule, and an optimizer uses them to update weights. The learning rate controls step size. Lower forecast loss does not directly optimize Sharpe ratio, drawdown, costs, or portfolio decisions.

core.title: Training passes are not evidence of generalization
core.text: One epoch processes the training dataset once; mini-batches permit multiple parameter updates within an epoch. Batch size affects gradient noise, memory, and compute, rather than network width. Falling training loss alongside rising validation loss suggests overfitting. Dropout, weight penalties, early stopping, and simpler baselines can improve model selection, but none guarantees profitable future trades.

groups.title: Neural-Network Structure
rules: Distinguish input, hidden, and output layers and specify their connectivity.
Count depth separately from layer width.
Interpret outputs according to the modeled target and objective.
traps: Equal hidden-unit totals do not imply equal parameter counts.
Adding units that contribute nothing need not change the function.

groups.title: Activations and Nonlinearity
rules: An affine map is a weighted sum plus bias; stacked affine maps remain affine.
Nonlinear activations allow nonlinear composition.
Saturated activations can reduce gradient flow without stopping forward computation.
traps: Bias terms alone do not introduce nonlinear input-output behavior.
Hidden-unit responses are not proof of causal economic meaning.

groups.title: Forward Propagation and Prediction
rules: Apply fitted preprocessing and the learned parameters during the forward pass.
Ordinary inference does not require labels, gradient calculation, or weight updates.
Separate the network score from the rule converting it to a trade.
traps: A threshold change need not change the weights or score.
A 0.70 score does not prove calibration in every market regime.

groups.title: Loss Functions and Learning Objectives
rules: Match the loss to the output and target: continuous value or class probability.
Assess how large errors and weighting influence the objective.
Evaluate portfolio economics separately from statistical prediction loss.
traps: MSE does not directly maximize Sharpe ratio or minimize drawdown.
Identical input features do not force identical learning objectives.

groups.title: Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
rules: Compute gradients through the full computation graph using the chain rule.
A gradient-descent optimizer moves opposite the gradient, scaled by a learning rate.
Use training and validation evidence to assess unstable or slow optimization.
traps: Backpropagation calculates derivatives; the optimizer applies updates.
One zero derivative is not proof of a global optimum.

groups.title: Epochs, Batches, and Training Dynamics
rules: One epoch is a complete dataset pass under the stated sampling scheme.
Mini-batch learning can update once per batch, many times per epoch.
Track training and validation curves and select checkpoints by the development protocol.
traps: Batch size does not count neurons.
More epochs can increase memorization and worsen held-out performance.

groups.title: Capacity, Overfitting, and Regularization
rules: Assess capacity relative to data quantity, quality, and deployment shift.
Use dropout, L2 penalties, or early stopping when supported by validation.
Compare simpler baselines and account for computational requirements.
traps: Near-zero training loss does not guarantee durable market structure.
No universal million-observation cutoff defines when neural networks can be used.

formulas.name: Dense layer
formulas.conditions: Dimensions and activation choices define the architecture. The output layer may use a different activation or no nonlinear activation.

formulas.name: Dense parameter count
formulas.conditions: Assumes every input connects to every output and there is one trainable bias per output unit.

formulas.name: MSE and L2-regularized objective
formulas.conditions: Penalty factors such as 1/2 and whether biases are penalized are implementation conventions. Choose λ using development data.

formulas.name: Gradient descent
formulas.conditions: η is the optimizer learning rate; a large step need not reduce a nonlinear loss.

formulas.name: Batches per epoch
formulas.conditions: Assumes one pass without replacement, retaining the final partial batch. If partial batches are dropped, use floor(N/B).

examples.title: Count a small dense network
examples.prompt: Three inputs feed four hidden units, which feed one scalar output. Include one bias per hidden and output unit.
examples.work: Input-to-hidden weights: 3×4 = 12; hidden biases: 4. Hidden-to-output weights: 4×1 = 4; output bias: 1. Total = 12+4+4+1 = 21.
examples.result: Four hidden units form one hidden layer; the network has 21 parameters under these assumptions.

examples.title: Compute an optimizer step
examples.prompt: A scalar parameter is 2.0, its loss derivative is +3.0, and the gradient-descent learning rate is 0.1.
examples.work: θ_new = 2.0 − 0.1×3.0 = 1.7. The positive derivative means increasing θ locally raises loss; gradient descent moves the other way.
examples.result: The new parameter is 1.7; this local step is not a global-optimality certificate.

examples.title: Count updates, then choose the checkpoint
examples.prompt: There are 10,000 observations, batches of 100, and one update per batch. Validation loss bottoms near epoch 40 but training continues to epoch 200.
examples.work: Each epoch has 10,000/100 = 100 batches. By epoch 40 there are 4,000 updates; by epoch 200, 20,000. More updates do not override the validation evidence.
examples.result: A development-selected checkpoint near epoch 40 may generalize better than the final weights.

core.title: Time order and availability define the forecasting problem
core.text: Lagged sequences can contain useful order information and are often statistically dependent, especially when windows overlap. Chronological evaluation better represents forecasting later periods from earlier evidence. Match feature timestamps to when data were released, including revisions; valid timing removes one failure mode but does not guarantee stability under a new regime.

core.title: Convolution and recurrence represent different structure
core.text: A temporal convolution reuses a local filter across ordered positions. Depth, kernel width, dilation, and pooling determine its effective receptive field; global pooling may remove precise position. A recurrent model carries hidden state forward and reuses update parameters through time. Long-range gradients can weaken, and recurrent state must be deliberately reset or initialized at independent sequence boundaries.

core.title: Attention connects positions through learned relevance
core.text: Self-attention can directly connect distant positions using data-dependent weights. A standard content-only attention mechanism needs positional information to explicitly represent sequence order; masks must enforce which information each forecast may access. Attention weights can reveal associations used in a computation but are not, by themselves, causal explanations or proof that irrelevant inputs are ignored.

core.title: Generative fluency is not factual or trading validation
core.text: LLMs can summarize filings, extract draft themes, and generate research text, but may omit qualifications or invent details. Retrieval adds candidate evidence and citations make it traceable; neither guarantees that the cited passage supports the claim. Verify consequential numbers, dates, and statements against sources, then separately test any trading decision rule after costs.

core.title: Responsible operation requires observable behavior and accountability
core.text: Aggregate accuracy can conceal subgroup errors and historical selection effects. Feature-attribution tools need fidelity and stability checks and do not establish causal effects. Deployment needs defined owners, version records, drift and incident monitoring, escalation, and intervention appropriate to the task. A successful backtest, a dollar limit, or unchanged code cannot guarantee that later decisions remain suitable.

groups.title: Time-Series and Sequential Modeling
rules: Preserve meaningful temporal order and use only information available at the forecast time.
Recognize overlap and dependence between adjacent windows.
Evaluate chronologically and assess performance under later regimes.
traps: A fixed-length window does not imply IID samples.
A revised value’s reference date is not its publication date.

groups.title: Convolutional Models for Financial Sequences
rules: Convolution shares local filter parameters across ordered positions and input channels.
Stacking, dilation, and pooling determine access to wider context.
Global pooling can retain motif strength while discarding exact location.
traps: Convolution is not invariant to arbitrary day reorderings.
ML2-D10G2Q3 E has a reverse-key contradiction: more channels guarantee neither generalization nor causality; read the issue note.

groups.title: Recurrent and Memory-Based Models
rules: A recurrent hidden state carries information from prior inputs.
Reused recurrence parameters allow order-dependent sequence processing.
Reset or deliberately initialize hidden state when starting an independent sequence.
traps: Longer input sequences do not guarantee learning of distant dependencies.
Gated memory mechanisms help gradient flow but do not guarantee perfect memory.

groups.title: Attention and Transformers
rules: Attention can form direct relationships between distant representations.
Provide a valid representation of temporal position and enforce forecast-time information boundaries.
Interpret attention as model association rather than proof of causation.
traps: Attention does not automatically exclude future targets.
Removing explicit positions is not equivalent to adding recurrent memory.

groups.title: Generative AI and Large Language Models
rules: Use generated text as an output to check, not an assumed verified source.
Assess retrieval relevance and confirm whether citations entail the associated claims.
Evaluate predictive and portfolio value independently of formatting quality.
traps: A syntactically valid BUY label demonstrates no trading edge.
Supplying a document does not guarantee every generated sentence is supported.

groups.title: Hallucination, Verification, and Human Oversight
rules: Verify material claims and numbers against the cited original source.
Use automated checks and human review with explicit ownership for consequential outputs.
Provide anomaly escalation and intervention mechanisms for autonomous actions.
traps: Polished writing is not a reliable confidence measure.
A position or dollar cap addresses only some failure modes.

groups.title: Bias, Explainability, and Responsible Deployment
rules: Inspect relevant subgroup performance as well as aggregate metrics.
Assess explanation stability and fidelity without assuming causality.
Maintain versions, monitoring thresholds, owners, and incident-response procedures.
traps: Removing protected attributes does not remove correlated proxies.
A one-time backtest does not establish perpetual suitability.

formulas.name: One-dimensional convolution
formulas.conditions: Illustrates a width-k filter across C aligned channels. Select an input window and padding/mask so the computation cannot see unavailable future data.

formulas.name: Single-filter parameter count
formulas.conditions: One output filter with C input channels, width k, and one bias; the same parameters are reused at each position.

formulas.name: Recurrent update
formulas.formula: h_t = φ(W_x x_t + W_h h_(t−1) + b)
formulas.conditions: A basic RNN illustration; gated models add state and gates. Reset boundaries should match independent sequences.

formulas.name: Scaled dot-product attention
formulas.conditions: M masks disallowed positions. Positional information and valid input construction remain necessary; attention weights are not causal effects.

examples.title: Convolution shares parameters
examples.prompt: A single width-five filter spans three channels of a 20-day sequence. Use stride one, valid padding, and one bias.
examples.work: Parameters = 5×3 + 1 = 16. Valid output positions = 20−5+1 = 16. The same 16 parameters are reused at all 16 positions. Global pooling could collapse those positions into one summary.
examples.result: Local parameter sharing is efficient; it does not guarantee generalization or preserve exact motif location.

examples.title: Verify the actual debt reduction
examples.prompt: A generated report says debt fell 40%. The cited filing instead reports a decline from $100 million to $86 million.
examples.work: Debt change = $86M − $100M = −$14M. Reduction = $14M/$100M = 14%. A 40% reduction would imply $60M remaining, which the filing does not support.
examples.result: Correct the figure to 14% and verify the source before using the report.

examples.title: Respect release time
examples.prompt: Forecast day t+1 using information available at the close of t. An economic statistic describes month t but its revised value was released on t+3.
examples.work: The statistic’s period label does not make the revision observable at t. Use the vintage actually released by t or omit the value. A causal attention mask cannot repair an input column already filled with the future revision.
examples.result: Enforce point-in-time availability before constructing model inputs.

issues.statement: Adding channels changes the available input information but guarantees neither generalization nor causality.
issues.detail: The stem asks for True when a claim is incorrect and False when it is correct. Statement E correctly says that adding channels changes available inputs but guarantees neither generalization nor causality. The official key nevertheless marks True and calls it incorrect, while its own rationale says more inputs can help or hurt and the architecture does not establish causality. The rationale supports the statement, so the logically consistent reverse selection is False. Preserve official True for pool scoring and distinguish it from the conceptual answer.

selfTests.prompt: A charging controller sees battery 30%, chooses recharge, then receives reward −2 for delay and later +12 for completing a delivery. Identify state, action, and reward, and explain why the −2 does not alone condemn the action.
selfTests.answer: Battery level is part of state; recharge is the chosen action; −2 and +12 are rewards from outcomes. The recharge changes future feasibility, so evaluate its cumulative consequences, not only the immediate delay cost.

selfTests.prompt: Action A pays 3 now then leads to a state valued at 4. Action B pays 0 now and leads to value 12 with probability 0.25 or value 2 with probability 0.75. With γ = 0.8, which has the higher one-step value?
selfTests.answer: A: 3 + 0.8×4 = 6.2. B successor expectation: 0.25×12 + 0.75×2 = 4.5; B total = 0.8×4.5 = 3.6. A has the greater value under these continuation estimates.

selfTests.prompt: Old Q = 4, reward = −1, max successor Q = 6, α = 0.25, γ = 0.5. Compute the nonterminal update. What if the same reward instead ends the episode?
selfTests.answer: Nonterminal target = −1+0.5×6 = 2; new Q = 4+0.25×(2−4) = 3.5. If terminal, target = −1 and new Q = 4+0.25×(−1−4) = 2.75. The reset state supplies no future value to a terminal transition.

selfTests.prompt: There are four actions, two tied for largest Q. Epsilon is 0.20; exploration is uniform over all four, and the greedy branch breaks its tie uniformly. What is the probability of each tied action and each other action?
selfTests.answer: Each tied action gets 0.80/2 + 0.20/4 = 0.45. Each nongreedy action gets 0.20/4 = 0.05. The four probabilities sum to 1. Setting epsilon to zero would still leave random tie-breaking.

selfTests.prompt: A Dyna agent observes 80 real transitions and performs 15 planning updates after each. A modeled pair has 12 visits to A and 8 to B. How many Q-updates occur, and what model probabilities should be used?
selfTests.answer: There are 80 direct and 80×15 = 1,200 planning updates, totaling 1,280 Q-updates but only 80 real transitions. For the pair, T(A)=12/20=0.6 and T(B)=8/20=0.4; repeated planning does not add independent observations to those counts.

selfTests.prompt: Three indicators have 4, 5, and 6 bins; holdings has three categories and there are three actions. How large is the nominal Q-table, and what does doubling only the first indicator’s bins do?
selfTests.answer: States = 4×5×6×3 = 360; entries = 360×3 = 1,080. Doubling only the first dimension gives 720 states and 2,160 entries. Finer detail doubles nominal data requirements for equal visits per entry but does not guarantee that all combinations are reachable or useful.

selfTests.prompt: A portfolio is short 400 shares and requests a long target of 400 shares. Starting value is $50,000; ending value before a $15 commission is $50,200. Find the order, net dollar reward, and net percentage return.
selfTests.answer: Buy 400−(−400)=800 shares. Net ending value is $50,185; reward = $185. Return = $185/$50,000 = 0.0037 = 0.37%, assuming no other costs or external cash flows.

selfTests.prompt: An RL system beats a tree in a later period, but RL sees holdings, has zero impact costs, and was selected from 30 variants using that period. What must change before attributing the edge to the algorithm?
selfTests.answer: Align information access across the complete pipelines, execution and cost assumptions, and capital/constraints. Treat the period used to select among 30 variants as development data and evaluate the finalized systems on an untouched later holdout with common metrics and benchmarks.

selfTests.prompt: A dense network has two inputs, three hidden units, one output, and a bias per unit. How many parameters does it have? With 1,200 training rows and batches of 80, how many updates occur in four epochs?
selfTests.answer: Parameters = 2×3+3 + 3×1+1 = 13. Batches per epoch = 1,200/80 = 15; four epochs give 60 updates if each batch triggers one update. Neither the parameter count nor the update count proves generalization.

selfTests.prompt: A recurrent model forecasts a company from past filings, but carries its hidden state over from an unrelated company; an LLM then cites a genuine filing for a wrong percentage. Identify the two independent checks.
selfTests.answer: Reset or deliberately initialize recurrent state at independent company boundaries so the intended sequence determines the forecast. Separately verify the generated percentage against the cited source and recompute it; a genuine citation does not guarantee that the claim is supported.
